archetype.name: Rookie Developmental (backup)
archetype.definition: An undrafted 25-year-old rookie pressed into emergency duty, working almost entirely underneath and not yet able to make the short game produce.

report.headline: Two emergency outings, 39 attempts, nothing to build on yet
report.take:
Joe Fagnano is the Ravens' third-string-turned-second-string quarterback. He is an undrafted rookie out of Maine and UConn, and he got onto the field only because Lamar Jackson's thumb broke the depth chart. He has played twice. At Buffalo in Week 8 he came on in relief in a game Jackson started and played 40% of the snaps. In Week 9 he started at home against Jacksonville on four days' rest. Baltimore lost those games 10-36 and 10-33. In Week 10 the team went back to Tyler Huntley, and the depth chart now lists Fagnano as QB2. That is the season so far: a backup who got a look and handed the job back.

The numbers are as bad as a 39-attempt sample can be. He is at -0.495 EPA per dropback, 51st of 54 qualifiers. His 0.77 adjusted net yards per dropback is last. He has three interceptions, a 7.7% interception rate that ranks 52nd, and two turnover-worthy fumbles. What drives it is the shape of the passing game. His intended air yards sit at 3.89, and the average throw lands 5.32 yards short of the sticks. Eleven of his 39 charted attempts went behind the line, and those cost -0.804 EPA apiece. Nearly all of the damage came on throws under 10 yards: -16.3 EPA there against -0.3 on the six throws past 10. The Ravens built him a quick, safe plan, and he couldn't complete the safe throws. His CPOE on short passes is -13.9.

Some of that is circumstance. Buffalo pressured him on 52% of his dropbacks and blitzed him 13 times in a partial game. More than half his plays came while trailing by nine or more, where defenses sit on the underneath routes. The Jacksonville start is the more damning tape. He was pressured only 25% of the time and his bad-throw rate fell to 6.7%, yet he still posted -11.9 EPA with two interceptions. A clean pocket did not fix the decisions. Zay Flowers, his best receiver, drew nine targets that came out to -1.624 EPA each, which is where most of the bleeding is. Mark Andrews was the one target who returned positive value.

Where it's heading: nowhere soon. Jackson's return is estimated for late December, Huntley has the starts until then, and Kedon Slovis is the emergency No. 3 behind Fagnano. Fagnano's 2026 is likely to be a clipboard and maybe some garbage-time series. With no career history to lean on, these 39 attempts are a first impression, not a verdict. It is a poor first impression.

strengths.title: Pressure doesn't automatically become sacks
strengths.body: For a rookie seeing pressure on more than four in ten dropbacks, he turned a relatively low share of it into sacks, 11th of 42. He also found an exit with his legs when he left the pocket. Both of his scrambles gained positive EPA, and one moved the chains. It is a small sample, but it suggests he is not frozen when the pocket collapses.

strengths.title: Throws past 10 yards held up
strengths.body: The handful of times he pushed the ball 10-plus yards, he was roughly on expectation (CPOE 0.2) and successful on half the plays. Six attempts is a hint, not a skill. Still, it argues the conservative plan around him may have been part of the problem rather than the cure.

concerns.title: Turnovers even from a clean pocket
concerns.body: Three interceptions in 39 attempts produce a 7.7% interception rate, 52nd of 54, and he added two turnover-worthy fumbles. Two of those interceptions came in the Jacksonville start, when he was pressured only a quarter of the time and his bad-throw rate was low. That points to reads and decisions rather than protection. This is the flaw that got him benched.

concerns.title: Short game that loses ground
concerns.body: The offense lived behind and just past the line, with an intended depth of 3.89 yards that sits well short of the sticks. Those throws need near-perfect accuracy to work, and he was 15.6 points under expected behind the line. Partly this is scheme protecting a rookie, partly game script while trailing. Either way, the plan ran up negative EPA play after play.

concerns.title: No connection with Flowers
concerns.body: His top wideout drew nine targets at -1.624 EPA each, by far the worst return of any receiver. The other targets were roughly break-even or better, so the problem is concentrated on the throws that should be his safest high-volume option. With so few reps together, chemistry is unlikely to improve while he sits at QB2.

trend.note: Both outings were deeply negative: -9.4 EPA in relief at Buffalo and -11.9 in the Jacksonville start. Cleaner protection in the second game didn't change the result, and Huntley took the Week 10 start.

nextGame.headline: Soft Carolina pass rush, but he's holding the clipboard
nextGame.body:
On paper Carolina is a forgiving matchup for any Baltimore quarterback. It ranks last in the league in both quarterback hit rate and sack rate, and 23rd in pass EPA allowed. It is also missing two cornerbacks who play most snaps, Will Lee III and Mike Jackson, plus linebacker Bobby Okereke. The catch for a dink-and-dunk passer is that the Panthers allow the second-lowest explosive pass rate, so this defense lets you have the short stuff and then tackles. Baltimore is a 2.5-point underdog with a 43.5 total.

The availability that matters most is Fagnano's own role. He is QB2 behind Huntley, who started Week 10, and Jackson is on IR with an estimated late-December return. He plays only if Huntley is hurt or benched, or if the game gets out of hand. Up front, starting guard Olaivavega Ioane (91% of snaps) left Monday's game with a shoulder issue. Without him, the protection that buckled at Buffalo gets thinner for whichever quarterback plays.

keyMatchups.title: League's weakest pass rush
keyMatchups.body: Carolina hits and sacks quarterbacks less than anyone. That would remove the Buffalo-style pressure that wrecked his first outing. It would also test whether his problems were really about the pocket, since the Jacksonville tape says they weren't.

keyMatchups.title: Depleted Carolina secondary
keyMatchups.body: Two regular corners are out, which should open the intermediate windows where his tiny sample was respectable. The Panthers still limit explosive passes, so the yards have to come in chunks of 10 to 15, not shots.

keyMatchups.title: Ioane's shoulder
keyMatchups.body: A 91%-snap guard left the Chargers game questionable. Baltimore already ranks 24th in hit rate allowed. Interior protection matters most for a quarterback whose game is built on quick, rhythm throws.

nextGame.watch: Whether Huntley holds the job. Fagnano only matters here if Huntley is injured or pulled.

restOfSeason.body:
Expect very little. Huntley is the starter until Jackson's estimated late-December return, and Fagnano sits behind him. His realistic weekly range runs from zero snaps to a relief appearance; my projections of 0 to 90 passing yards and 0 to 1 interception a game span exactly that. If he is forced into a start, the Week 9 profile is the baseline: a quick, short plan that only works if his underneath accuracy improves from where it has been.

Some regression toward average is likely if he gets more reps. A 7.7% interception rate and a -0.804 EPA on screens and swings are extreme even for a rookie backup, and the Flowers numbers rest on nine targets. But nothing in the sample shows a strength the Ravens can build a game plan around. The most hopeful reading is that this was an undrafted rookie thrown in against a top-five defense on a short week. That reading is reasonable, but 39 attempts can't confirm it.
swingFactors: Timing of Lamar Jackson's return from IR

confidence.note: 39 attempts over two games, no career history, and he is currently a backup.
